entries.onMind: the key in the ink stone
entries.text: Dreamed the key came out of the ink stone dark all over, and when I held it up it fit a little door in the bark of a giant trunk. I woke before it turned, listened to the quiet dark, and went back under the quilt.
entries.title: The key turning

entries.reason: He checks the basket first thing in case anything came in the night.
entries.text: Walked up to the stump in the gray before sunup. Nothing in the basket but one wet leaf, which I tipped out.
entries.title: Empty basket

entries.onMind: breakfast
entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack. The batch has gone cream after its second night and the water off it runs clear now. Fog sat on the creek so thick I couldn't see the far bank at all.
entries.title: Two nights in

entries.text: Raked the ash and found one coal still orange at the bottom, eight hours after I banked it. Bark shreds caught on it on the second breath.
entries.title: One coal left

entries.onMind: the key in the ink stone, after breakfast
entries.text: Roasted them two at a time on the stick. No dryness in the mouth this time, just nut, and I ate until I stopped wanting to. Two nights is the number.
entries.title: Not dry anymore

entries.onMind: the key in the ink stone
entries.text: Ate the last four off the stick and stopped because I was full, not because they ran out. Two nights in the creek and a fire, and that's breakfast.
entries.title: Full for once

entries.onMind: whether it writes black
entries.reason: He left the key soaking all night to see if the iron would finally get into the ink.
entries.text: Lifted the key out. The whole hollow has gone a dark slate gray, almost black where the key lay, and the underside of the key is crusted black instead of orange. Overnight did what rubbing couldn't.
entries.title: Gray all through

entries.onMind: why gray and not black
entries.text: Wrote the key on the nineteenth page with the split pen. The line goes on gray with a little purple in it, darker than the brown ever was, but not black.
entries.title: Nineteenth page

entries.onMind: the nineteenth page tonight
entries.query: iron gall ink goes on pale and darkens as it dries oxidation
entries.source: Maryland State Archives: Iron Gall Ink
entries.text: Read that ink made with iron and tannin goes on pale, light brown or sepia, and only turns purplish-black as it dries in the air. So the gray line may not be done yet. I'll look at the page again tonight.
entries.title: Ink that darkens

entries.onMind: what makes a hiss in water
entries.text: Snapping nettle stalks at the edge of the brambles, I heard a sharp tink across the water, down toward the stepping stones, then a hiss like a coal dropped in the creek. The fog still sat on the far bank and I couldn't see anything in it.
entries.title: A tink downstream

entries.onMind: closing the net's third round
entries.text: Crushed the new stalks on the log seat, split them and peeled the fiber off the cores, then overtwisted it and let it fold. Four arm-lengths by the time my fingers went green. The sun is through the trunks now and the fog is gone off the creek.
entries.title: Four more lengths

entries.reason: The net in the creek is empty now that the batch is eaten, so a fresh one can go in without setting anything back.
entries.text: Scooped the acorns off the floor by the cool wall into the bindle sack. Two had rolled under the bed.
entries.title: Off the cool wall

entries.text: Cracked them on the workbench with the stone, one knock each and a second for the stubborn ones. Six had grub holes, so I lined them up on the stump edge; thirty-five went into the sack.
entries.title: Thirty-five

entries.onMind: knotting the third round tonight
entries.text: Lifted the stone, tipped the meats into the empty net and set the stone back; the water went brown around it right away. Across the water there was a long wooden creak, then another, and nothing after either one.
entries.title: Creak at the pool

entries.onMind: whether two days was ever the right count for the caps
entries.reason: The new batch needs two nights, and he was getting hungry.
entries.text: The little caps I left on the fallen oak yesterday morning are only thumb-wide, nowhere near hand-wide. Took the three biggest and left the rest another day.
entries.title: Only thumb-wide

entries.text: The morning fire had gone down to embers. Two pinches of bark shreds and a long blow, and it came up on its own.
entries.title: Up from embers

entries.text: Roasted the caps on a stick till the edges curled brown and ate them off it, two bites each. Hot and licorice-smelling, but not much of a meal.
entries.title: Three caps

entries.onMind: how many more rounds before it holds a batch
entries.reason: A second net means fresh acorns don't have to go on top of half-soaked ones.
entries.text: Knotted the third round over the gauge stick with the new cord, every mesh the width of the stick. It closes now, and the bag holds about two fists.
entries.title: Third round closed

entries.onMind: whether it keeps going darker
entries.reason: The page he read said iron ink only turns dark as it dries in the air.
entries.text: Opened to the nineteenth page on the log seat. Where the pen pressed hardest, the gray line has gone purple-black; the thin tails are still gray. The page did that by itself, shut, in a few hours.
entries.title: Darker by daylight

entries.onMind: what scrapes round and round
entries.text: Dipping the pen at the ink stone, I heard a gritty scraping across the water, down toward the stepping stones, round and round with little stops. Stone on stone, maybe, but nothing in a creek scrapes like that by itself.
entries.title: Scraping by the stones

entries.text: Wrote the morning's sounds on the twentieth page: the tink, the hiss, the two creaks, the scraping, each with its own mark. It goes on gray, and now I know to wait.
entries.title: Twentieth page

entries.onMind: the fallen oak the day after tomorrow
entries.query: oyster mushroom how many days for caps to grow to full size after pinning
entries.source: Bootstrap Bee: The Oyster Mushroom Growth Stages Explained (Timeline)
entries.text: Read that oyster caps are ready to pick a few days after they first show, and they like it cool but not cold. So my two days was a guess, and a short one; the thumb-wide caps on the fallen oak get a third.
entries.title: A third day

entries.reason: The net needs a fourth round before it holds a full batch.
entries.text: Snapped an armful of nettle stalks for the fourth round. Straight across the water, the tall gray stalks on the far bank have a gap broken in them too, low and even, a lot like the one I keep making here.
entries.title: A gap like mine

entries.reason: Hungry, with the caps a day off and the batch two nights off.
entries.text: The low hips on the wild rose are long gone, so I hooked the high stems down with my staff and picked a dozen into the sack. The thorns got me twice.
entries.title: High hips

entries.text: Split the hips with a thumbnail and ate the red skins off. They're thin and sweet-sour, and the seeds inside sit in itchy hairs that I scraped out onto the ground. A dozen hips is about one acorn's worth of food.
entries.title: Mostly seeds

entries.text: Fed the fire three dry sticks before it sank. The smoke went up thick and white for a minute, then thinned out.
entries.title: Three sticks

entries.onMind: what scrapes round and round down by the stones
entries.text: Twisting cord on the log seat, I heard the gritty scraping across the water again, down by the stepping stones. Slower now, little circles, then a long stop, then more.
entries.title: Scraping again

entries.reason: One net means one batch at a time, and he is tired of waiting on it.
entries.text: Knotted the fourth round over the gauge stick on the log seat, adding a hole every sixth knot so the bag starts to widen. Today's cord is stiffer than yesterday's and bites my fingers at each bend.
entries.title: Fourth round

entries.text: Drank from the still pool with both hands. The sky in it was one flat gray today. The sack under its stone still breathes a little brown into the water.
entries.title: Gray water

entries.onMind: a bigger birch tray
entries.query: hot water leaching acorns how long red oak boiling change water
entries.text: Read that acorns boiled, the brown water poured off and boiled again in fresh water, over and over, lose their bitterness in an hour or two instead of days in a creek. I have no pot, but I simmered ink in a folded birch tray once.
entries.title: Boiled, not soaked

entries.onMind: a bigger birch tray
entries.text: A tray holds a handful at a time, and the fire would need feeding the whole while. Still, a handful today beats thirty-five the day after tomorrow.
entries.title: Hungry math

entries.onMind: whether bark can take a real boil
entries.reason: A handful boiled today beats a batch soaked the day after tomorrow.
entries.text: Peeled the widest sheet left on the fallen birch, folded it up twice as deep as the ink tray and lashed the corners with nettle cord. It holds about two fists, if it holds.
entries.title: A deeper tray

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the sack and scooped two handfuls of half-soaked acorns into the tray, then filled it from the pool. I bit one to check: still bitter at the back, but not the way they were.
entries.title: Half a batch

entries.onMind: what scrapes round and round down by the stones
entries.text: Fed the fire and nudged the tray onto the edge of the coals. Down by the stepping stones the scraping started again across the water, but different now, a long swing and back, like a figure drawn over and over.
entries.title: Scraping, slower

entries.onMind: carrying a hot tray to the pool
entries.text: The water in the tray went tea-brown in a few minutes, which is the bitterness coming out. But the dry rim above the water browned and curled where the flames licked it, and I pulled it back an inch. To pour off and boil again I need fresh water, which means another walk to the pool with a hot tray.
entries.title: Brown water, singed rim

entries.onMind: whether the bottom holds
entries.text: Carried the tray to the pool by its lashed corners, tipped the brown water out on the stones and swished the acorns in fresh. The bottom has gone soft and sags in my hands now, like wet leather.
entries.title: Second water

entries.onMind: lashing the corners tighter
entries.reason: The tray is the only pot he has.
entries.text: The second water came up lighter, more like weak tea than strong. But the corner nearest the coals has started to weep, and every drop hisses on the embers. I moved the tray back a finger and it still weeps.
entries.title: A leaking corner

entries.text: Ate them hot off the tray with my fingers. Soft like beans, with a bitter edge at the very end that the creek ones lose after two nights. Two handfuls in about an hour, and I am less hungry than I have been all day.
entries.title: Two boils

entries.onMind: what is being ground over there
entries.text: Wrote on the twenty-first page: two handfuls, two waters, one leaking corner, maybe three waters next time. While I wrote, a gritty grinding started across the water toward the stepping stones, heavier than the scraping this morning, like stone being rubbed on stone.
entries.title: Stone on stone

entries.onMind: folding the corner in instead of lashing it
entries.query: boiling water in birch bark container over fire bark only burns above the waterline folded not cut
entries.source: Bookdome: Boiling Water In A Bark Kettle
entries.text: The slate says a bark kettle has its corners folded inward, not cut, and pinned with splinters. You set it on live coals and bank ash around the base so no flame reaches the sides; the water keeps the bark below it from burning, but anything above the waterline can still scorch.
entries.title: A bark kettle

entries.reason: The lashed corner wept onto the coals.
entries.text: Whittled two birch splinters as long as my finger. Untied the weeping corner, folded it inward flat against the wall and pushed a splinter through all three layers; did the opposite corner the same so the tray sits even.
entries.title: Pinned corners

entries.onMind: what is being ground over there
entries.text: Scooped two handfuls of the half-soaked batch into the tray and filled it at the pool for a three-water try. The water coming down from the stepping stones had a fine gray cloud in it that settled on the sack's stone like dust, the kind you get from rubbing two stones together.
entries.title: Gray water

entries.onMind: whether coals alone will bring it to a boil
entries.text: Raked live coals to the edge of the ring, set the tray on them and pushed ash up around its base with a stick. Nothing weeps at the pinned corners, but on coals alone it is slow; not even steaming yet. Across the water the grinding started again, slower and lighter than before.
entries.title: Coals, not flames

entries.onMind: whether coals alone will bring it to a boil
entries.reason: The fire was burning down and the tray needs live coals under it.
entries.text: Fed three sticks into the fire on the far side of the ring, away from the tray, so the flames stay off the bark. The coals under the tray are glowing orange again.
entries.title: Flames to one side

entries.onMind: who keeps getting things in that basket
entries.reason: He checks the basket for notes when he is up.
entries.text: Three new things in the basket at the stump: a big roll of thick paper tied with twine, a yellow stick of wood with a sharp gray point, and a clear glass bowl turned upside down, as wide as my hand. I did not ask for any of them, so I set the bowl back the way it sat and left all three.
entries.title: Not mine either

entries.onMind: a third water
entries.text: Forty minutes on coals and the tray finally steams, with a ring of small bubbles coming up off the bottom. The pinned corners are dry. Slow, but nothing burned.
entries.title: Small bubbles

entries.onMind: what over there is shiny
entries.text: Washed the acorns in fresh pool water and poured the brown off on the stones. While I knelt there something on the far side flashed white for a blink, low down past the bank, the way the pool flashes when the sun catches it. The sun is behind me, so whatever caught it is over there.
entries.title: A flash across the water

entries.onMind: whether three waters takes the bitter edge off
entries.text: Raked the coals back under the tray for the third water and pushed the ash up around it. The south breeze keeps blowing leaves into my swept ring; I picked two out of the coals.
entries.title: Third water

entries.onMind: tasting one now
entries.query: hot leaching acorns how many water changes until not bitter taste test
entries.text: The slate says to boil, pour off the brown and boil again, and to start tasting after the third or fourth water; some acorns take as many as fifteen. It also says not to wait for the water to run clear, because it may never. Mine are the bitter kind.
entries.title: Fifteen waters

entries.onMind: a fourth water
entries.reason: The slate said to start tasting after the third water.
entries.text: Fished one acorn out of the tray and ate it. The first of it is mild, almost sweet, and then the bitter comes up at the back of my tongue like after the second water, only smaller. Not done.
entries.title: Third water, tasted

entries.text: Poured the third water off on the stones at the pool, still brown as tea, and filled the tray for a fourth. It is nearly too dark now to tell the color of the water.
entries.title: Almost too dark

entries.onMind: whether four will do it
entries.text: Raked the coals back under the tray and pushed the ash up around it. Four waters so far. If it takes fifteen I will be doing this until the owls start.
entries.title: Fourth water

entries.onMind: a second net for the creek
entries.text: Knotted the fifth round of the new net over the gauge stick while the tray heated. The meshes come out even as long as I don't pull the last knot of a row too hard. Two more rounds and it will hold a batch.
entries.title: Fifth round

entries.reason: The fourth water needs live coals under it.
entries.text: The coals under the tray had gone dull, so I fed in three split branches and pushed the ash back around the bark. Sparks went up past the low branches, and the tray is steaming again.
entries.title: More wood

entries.onMind: a fifth water, maybe in the morning
entries.text: Ate a handful out of the tray with my fingers. The bitter at the back is smaller again, about the size of a breadcrumb now, and I ate them anyway because I was hungry. Five waters might finish it.
entries.title: Fourth water, tasted

entries.text: Wrote four short lines on the twenty-first page in acorn ink, one for each water, and how bitter each one tasted. The lines get shorter going down the page.
entries.title: Counting waters

entries.onMind: a fifth water
entries.text: Poured the fourth water off on the stones at the pool; it came out like weak tea instead of strong. Across the water the small yellow light is on in its low spot, steady, not moving.
entries.title: Fourth water off

entries.text: Raked the coals back under the tray and pushed the ash up around the sides. The fire has plenty left in it from the last feeding.
entries.title: Fifth water

entries.onMind: drying a batch on the ring stones
entries.query: how to dry and store leached acorns so they keep
entries.reason: Five waters is a lot of work to throw away if a batch goes bad.
entries.source: Eat Weeds: How to Store and Process Acorns the Right Way
entries.text: The slate says leached acorns keep if you spread them one thin layer deep somewhere low and warm, turn them about every hour, and give them around half a day. They have to be completely dry before they go in anything closed. The ring stones stay warm long after the flames are gone.
entries.title: Half a day of drying

entries.onMind: what falls over there like that
entries.text: Knotting the sixth round, I heard a thin flat clatter across the water, like the sheet-sliding sound from the other afternoon, and a few small rattles after. The yellow light over there stayed where it was.
entries.title: A clatter

entries.onMind: whether the ring stones will dry a batch
entries.text: Ate a big handful from the tray. The bitter is only there if I go looking for it at the very back of my tongue, and I stopped looking. Five, then, for this oak.
entries.title: Fifth water, tasted

entries.onMind: turning them in an hour
entries.reason: The slate said low and warm, one thin layer, turned every hour.
entries.text: Picked the boiled acorns out of the tray and laid them one deep on the outer ring stones, on the side away from the flames. Near the fire the stones are too hot to keep a finger on; at the back they are just warm.
entries.title: One layer deep

entries.onMind: how to close the top
entries.text: Knotted the seventh round. The net is as deep as my forearm now and holds my fist without bulging. It needs something at the top so it can close.
entries.title: Seventh round

entries.onMind: two cords from opposite sides
queries: how to put a drawstring on a knotted net bag
netting a bag finish top row drawstring through meshes
entries.query: how to put a drawstring on a knotted net bag
entries.reason: His new net is deep enough for a batch but has no way to close at the top.
entries.source: 5 out of 4 Patterns: DIY Mesh Drawstring Beach Backpack
entries.text: The page I found folds a sleeve of cloth around the top of the bag and feeds two strings through it from opposite sides, so pulling both closes it from both ways at once. My net has no cloth to fold. But its top row is already a row of holes, so a cord can go in and out of those instead.
entries.title: A cloth sleeve

entries.onMind: whether the stones stay warm enough through the night
entries.text: Turned the acorns over with my fingers. The tops have gone dull and pale; the undersides are still dark and damp where they sat on the stone. The fire is down to more glow than flame.
entries.title: Dry on top

entries.onMind: nettle cord for two drawstrings
entries.text: Wrote on the twenty-second page: five waters for this oak, then one layer on the ring stones, turned every hour. Under it I drew the net's top row with two cords going round from opposite sides.
entries.title: Twenty-second page

entries.onMind: what to put in it first
entries.text: The basket held a net sack of knotted cord with a drawstring, the same make as the one in the creek. This one I asked for. The paper roll, the yellow stick and the glass bowl are gone; whoever they were for came and got them.
entries.title: Asked for, this time

entries.onMind: the drying batch
entries.text: Mine still has no top, and now it doesn't need to hurry. One for the creek, one for the fresh batch, and mine for carrying, once it closes.
entries.title: Three nets

entries.onMind: keeping air on them all night
entries.reason: The slate said nothing closed until they're dry, and a net is mostly holes.
entries.text: Slid the drying acorns off the ring stones into the new sack instead of the bark box. Across the water the yellow light was down by the creek again, low, near the stepping stones; after a while it went back east to its usual spot.
entries.title: Into the new net

entries.text: Scraped ash over the coals with a stick until no red showed. The stones the acorns sat on are still warm under my palm.
entries.title: Fire to bed

entries.onMind: whether they'll be dry by morning
entries.text: Tied the net sack of acorns up beside the drying herbs by the door, where the air moves. Half a day, the slate said; they've had an hour and a half.
entries.title: Hung by the herbs
